## Learning goals

This chapter is about measurement: how economists turn millions of transactions into a few
numbers that describe a whole economy. By the end of it you will be able to:

- derive why **production = expenditure = income**: value added adds up to final sales, and the
  national income identity $Y = C + I + G + NX$ splits GDP by who buys it;
- describe how the composition of U.S. GDP and **labor's share** of income have changed since 1929,
  and derive the labor-share measure that splits proprietors' income;
- derive the **Laspeyres**, **Paasche** and **chain-weighted** growth rates of real GDP as weighted
  averages, and split nominal growth into **inflation** and real growth;
- compare GDP across countries with exchange rates and **purchasing power parity**, and read the
  comparative statics of each conversion;
- read CSV files with pandas, compute new columns, work with dates, and draw area and line charts
  with Plotly Express;
- compare countries, and check that two data sources use the same definitions before you compare them.

The next cell defines a helper that only the book website needs. Run it and move on.

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig
```

The data figures of this chapter let you add other countries. On the website, a menu above each of
these figures adds a group of countries (the G7, a world region, ...); the next cell builds those menus.

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helpers for the website's country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_traces(data, y, skip, x="year", fmt=".1f", markers=False):
    """One line per country of a long table (country, x, y), leaving out the countries in skip."""
    extra = {}
    for name, part in data.groupby("country"):
        if name not in skip:
            extra[name] = [go.Scatter(x=part[x], y=part[y], name=name, mode="lines+markers" if markers else "lines",
                                      line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=2),
                                      hovertemplate=f"<b>{name}</b><br>%{{x}}: %{{y:{fmt}}}<extra></extra>")]
    return extra


def country_menu(fig, extra, countries):
    """Add the extra countries' traces hidden, and a menu that shows one group of them (G7, a region, ...).

    The traces already in fig (the textbook's) stay as they are, and slider steps only switch those."""
    n = len(fig.data)
    owner = []
    for name, traces in extra.items():
        for trace in traces:
            trace.visible = False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(name)
    groups = {"G7": countries.country[countries.g7], "G20": countries.country[countries.g20],
              "OECD": countries.country[countries.oecd]}
    for region in sorted(countries.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = countries.country[countries.region == region]
    rest, autoscale = list(range(n, len(fig.data))), {"yaxis.autorange": True}
    buttons = [dict(label="Textbook only", method="update", args=[{"visible": [False] * len(owner)}, autoscale, rest])]
    for label, members in groups.items():
        visible = [o in set(members) for o in owner]
        if any(visible):
            buttons.append(dict(label=f"+ {label} ({sum(visible)})", method="update", args=[{"visible": visible}, autoscale, rest]))
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=0, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        for step in slider.steps:
            step.args = [{"visible": list(step.args[0]["visible"])}, step.args[1], list(range(n))]
    return fig
```

```{python}
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Like slider_figure, but with a dropdown menu: one precomputed figure per value (e.g. per country)."""
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[values.index(start)].layout)
    owner = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (values[i] == start)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes], "yaxis": f.layout.yaxis.to_plotly_json(),
                  "xaxis": f.layout.xaxis.to_plotly_json()}
        if "yaxis2" in f.layout.to_plotly_json():       # a second vertical axis (Fig. 2)
            layout["yaxis2"] = f.layout.yaxis2.to_plotly_json()
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update", args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=values.index(start), x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig
```

## Model overview

This chapter has no model of behavior. Instead, it builds the measuring sticks that every later model is tested against. The main one is **gross domestic product** (GDP): the market value of all final goods and services that an economy produces in a given period. Three questions organize the chapter. How can one total be counted in three different ways and still give a single answer? How do we split a rise in GDP into higher prices and more goods? And how do we compare economies that use different currencies and face different prices?

Each question has an accounting framework, and this section derives them one by one. The first block shows why **production = expenditure = income**: value added, the national income identity and labor's share of income. The second block separates **nominal** from **real** GDP with the Laspeyres, Paasche and chain-weighted quantity indexes. The third turns the same tools into **price indexes and inflation** rates. The fourth converts GDP across countries with **exchange rates** and **purchasing power parity**. At the end, `### The model in code` turns the formulas into Python functions and checks every result with numbers, including the textbook's small economy of apples and computers (Table 2.4).

There are no parameters in this chapter, so no letter carries a bar. The subscript $t$ is the year, $i$ is a good and $j$ is a producer. A small $p_{i,t}$ and $q_{i,t}$ are the price and quantity of one good, and a capital $P_t$ is the price level of the whole economy. A $g$ is a growth rate. All the results below are **identities**: they hold in any data set, by the way the variables are defined. That is what makes them useful checks on the data.

<!-- cell -->

### Production, expenditure and income

#### Definitions

- A **final good** is bought by its last user: a household, a firm that keeps it as capital, the government, or a buyer abroad. An **intermediate good** is used up in making another good in the same period, like flour in bread or electricity in a factory.
- Producer $j$ sells its output for **revenue** $R_j$ and buys **intermediate inputs** worth $M_j$. Its **value added** is what it adds to the inputs it bought:
  $$VA_j \equiv R_j - M_j.$$
- **Capital** (buildings, machines, software) helps to produce output but is not used up within the period. Its wear and tear is **depreciation**. GDP is *gross* because depreciation is not subtracted; net domestic product is GDP minus depreciation.
- Value added is paid out as **income**: compensation of employees (wages, salaries and benefits), taxes on production less subsidies, depreciation, and the **net operating surplus**, what remains for the owners. The operating surplus is a residual, so the split always adds up to value added.
- **Spending** on final goods has four parts: consumption $C$; investment $I$ (business structures, equipment, intellectual property products such as software and R&D, new housing, and the change in inventories); government purchases $G$; and net exports $NX$, exports $X$ minus imports $IM$. Government *purchases* buy goods and services. Transfers such as pensions, and interest on the public debt, move income from one group to another and buy nothing, so they are not part of $G$.
- Only **new production** counts. The resale of a used good is not production, but the dealer's margin is: it pays for the service of finding a buyer.

#### Deriving the results

**Step 1: value added adds up to final sales.** Take a chain of $J$ producers. Producer 1 buys no inputs, every producer sells its whole output to the next one, and producer $J$ sells to final users. Then $M_1 = 0$ and $M_j = R_{j-1}$, so that

$$VA_1 = R_1, \qquad VA_2 = R_2 - R_1, \qquad \dots, \qquad VA_J = R_J - R_{J-1}.$$

Add them up. Every revenue except the last appears twice, once with a plus sign (as a seller's revenue) and once with a minus sign (as a buyer's cost), so the sum *telescopes*:

$$\sum_{j=1}^{J} VA_j = R_1 + (R_2 - R_1) + \dots + (R_J - R_{J-1}) = R_J.$$

The same cancellation happens in any web of sales between firms, because every sale of an intermediate good is revenue for one firm and a cost for another. So the production approach and the final-sales definition give the same GDP:

$$\text{GDP} = \sum_j VA_j = \text{value of the final goods and services}. \tag{1}$$

*Intuition.* Adding up all revenues would count the grain inside the bread twice, once when the farm sells it and again when the bakery sells the bread. Subtracting purchased inputs counts the contribution of each stage exactly once.

**Step 2: production = income.** Add the income split of value added over all producers:

$$\text{GDP} = \text{compensation} + \text{taxes on production less subsidies} + \text{net operating surplus} + \text{depreciation}.$$

Because the operating surplus is whatever is left over, each dollar of value added is somebody's income. In the data, though, the statisticians measure income from sources (tax records, payroll data) that differ from those they use for spending. The income total is called **gross domestic income** (GDI), and the small gap between GDI and GDP is the *statistical discrepancy*.

**Step 3: production = expenditure.** Final goods are bought by households, firms, the government and foreigners, so domestic buyers spend $C + I + G$ and foreign buyers spend $X$. But $C$, $I$ and $G$ also include goods made abroad, which are not domestic production. Subtracting them gives the domestic output that was sold to final users: $C + I + G + X - IM$. What about goods that were made but not sold this year? They are counted as **inventory investment**, part of $I$, as if the firm had bought its own output. So every unit produced has a buyer in the accounts, and

$$Y = C + I + G + NX, \qquad NX \equiv X - IM. \tag{2}$$

This is the **national income identity**, the expenditure approach to GDP $Y$.

**Step 4: shares of GDP.** Divide both sides of (2) by $Y$ ([Appendix C.2](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.2-percentages-ratios-and-index-numbers)):

$$1 = \frac{C}{Y} + \frac{I}{Y} + \frac{G}{Y} + \frac{NX}{Y}.$$

The four shares add up to 100 percent in every year. Now take the change of both sides between two years. The left side is always 1, so its change is zero:

$$\Delta\frac{C}{Y} + \Delta\frac{I}{Y} + \Delta\frac{G}{Y} + \Delta\frac{NX}{Y} = 0.$$

A rise in one share must be matched by a fall in the others (Fig. 2). We compute shares from *nominal* values; the second block explains why.

**Step 5: labor's share of income.** We want the fraction of income that pays for work. Two items do not belong cleanly to labor or to capital. Taxes on production $T$ (such as sales taxes) are income of neither. **Proprietors' income** $\mathit{Prop}$, what the self-employed earn, pays both for their own work and for their own equipment. Income net of these taxes is

$$\text{GDI} - T = \text{compensation} + \mathit{Prop} + \text{other capital income}.$$

Assume that labor's fraction of proprietors' income equals labor's fraction $\theta$ of all the other income:

$$\theta = \frac{\text{compensation}}{\text{GDI} - T - \mathit{Prop}}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \text{compensation} = \theta\,(\text{GDI} - T - \mathit{Prop}).$$

Labor's total income is then compensation plus the fraction $\theta$ of proprietors' income. Its share of income net of taxes is

$$\frac{\text{compensation} + \theta\,\mathit{Prop}}{\text{GDI} - T} = \frac{\theta\,(\text{GDI} - T - \mathit{Prop}) + \theta\,\mathit{Prop}}{\text{GDI} - T} = \frac{\theta\,(\text{GDI} - T)}{\text{GDI} - T} = \theta.$$

So the labor share is

$$\text{labor share} = \frac{\text{compensation}}{\text{GDI} - \text{taxes on production} - \text{proprietors' income}}, \tag{3}$$

and the capital share is one minus it. *Intuition.* Leaving proprietors out of both the top and the bottom of the fraction gives the same answer as splitting their income in the same proportion as everybody else's. The simple ratio compensation/GDP is lower, because its denominator still holds the taxes and all of proprietors' income. Fig. 3 uses equation (3).

#### What the framework predicts

The identities tell us exactly which entries move when something happens. A few examples, each worth $\$p$:

| Event | $C$ | $I$ | $G$ | $NX$ | GDP $Y$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A household buys a new car made at home | $+p$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | $+p$ |
| A household buys a new imported car | $+p$ | 0 | 0 | $-p$ | 0 |
| A firm builds a factory | 0 | $+p$ | 0 | 0 | $+p$ |
| A firm makes goods it cannot sell this year | 0 | $+p$ (inventories) | 0 | 0 | $+p$ |
| A foreigner buys a new car made at home | 0 | 0 | 0 | $+p$ | $+p$ |
| The government pays a pension | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| The government hires a teacher | 0 | 0 | $+p$ | 0 | $+p$ |
| A dealer resells a used car with margin $m$ | $+m$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | $+m$ |

- **Imports never add to GDP.** They enter $C$, $I$ or $G$ with a plus sign and $NX$ with a minus sign, so the two cancel.
- **The shares are tied together.** Since they add up to one, their changes add up to zero (Step 4). Over a decade, a rising consumption share has to be paid for by a lower share of something else.
- **GDP measures market production, not welfare.** It leaves out work done at home (cooking, caring for one's own children), the value of longer and healthier lives, leisure, and the depletion of natural resources and damage to the environment. The note on Table 2.3 in the Fig. 3 section discusses a broader measure that adds some of them.

<!-- cell -->

### Real GDP: quantity indexes and chain weighting

#### Definitions

The economy produces goods $i = 1, \dots, n$. Good $i$ has price $p_{i,t}$ and quantity $q_{i,t}$ in year $t$.

- **Nominal GDP** values each year's goods at that year's prices: $\text{nominal GDP}_t = \sum_i p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t}$.
- **Real GDP at the prices of a base year $b$** values each year's goods at the *same* prices: $\sum_i p_{i,b}\,q_{i,t}$. Prices are held fixed, so it changes only when quantities change. It is measured in "year-$b$ dollars".
- The **expenditure share** of good $i$ is $s_{i,t} \equiv p_{i,t}q_{i,t}\big/\sum_k p_{k,t}q_{k,t}$. The shares of a year add up to one.
- The **growth rate** of the quantity of good $i$ is $g_i$, so $q_{i,t+1} = (1+g_i)\,q_{i,t}$.

The **price level**, also called the **GDP deflator**, is defined as the ratio of nominal to real GDP, $P_t \equiv \text{nominal GDP}_t/\text{real GDP}_t$. Multiplying both sides by real GDP gives

$$\text{nominal GDP}_t = P_t \times \text{real GDP}_t. \tag{4}$$

With a single good, $P_t$ is simply its price and real GDP is its quantity. In the base year, real and nominal GDP are equal, so $P_b = 1$ (or 100, as an index).

#### Deriving the results

**Step 1: two ways to hold prices fixed.** To measure real growth from year $t$ to year $t+1$, we can value both years' quantities at the *initial* prices (the **Laspeyres** index) or at the *final* prices (the **Paasche** index):

$$1 + g^L = \frac{\sum_i p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t}}, \qquad 1 + g^P = \frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t}}.$$

**Step 2: Laspeyres growth is an average of the goods' growth rates.** In the numerator, replace $q_{i,t+1}$ by $(1+g_i)\,q_{i,t}$ and split the fraction good by good:

$$1 + g^L = \sum_i \frac{p_{i,t}\,q_{i,t}}{\sum_k p_{k,t}\,q_{k,t}}\,(1+g_i) = \sum_i s_{i,t}\,(1+g_i) = \sum_i s_{i,t} + \sum_i s_{i,t}\,g_i = 1 + \sum_i s_{i,t}\,g_i.$$

The last step uses the fact that the shares add up to one.

**Step 3: Paasche growth is an average too, with other weights.** Turn the Paasche fraction upside down and use $q_{i,t} = q_{i,t+1}/(1+g_i)$:

$$\frac{1}{1+g^P} = \frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t}}{\sum_k p_{k,t+1}\,q_{k,t+1}} = \sum_i \frac{p_{i,t+1}\,q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_k p_{k,t+1}\,q_{k,t+1}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+g_i} = \sum_i \frac{s_{i,t+1}}{1+g_i}.$$

Together:

$$g^L = \sum_i s_{i,t}\,g_i, \qquad \frac{1}{1+g^P} = \sum_i \frac{s_{i,t+1}}{1+g_i}. \tag{5}$$

*Intuition.* Both indexes average the growth rates of the individual goods. The Laspeyres index weights each good by its share of spending in the first year; the Paasche index (a weighted *harmonic* mean of the growth factors) uses the shares of the final year.

**When do the two agree?** (a) If every quantity grows at the same rate $g$, both formulas in (5) give exactly $g$, because the shares add up to one. (b) If every price changes by the same factor $\lambda$, so that $p_{i,t+1} = \lambda p_{i,t}$, then $\lambda$ cancels from the top and the bottom of the Paasche fraction, which becomes the Laspeyres fraction. So the two indexes differ only when **relative prices** change. The usual pattern is that the goods whose relative price falls, like computers, are the goods whose quantity grows fastest. At the initial prices those goods were still expensive and carry a large weight, so $g^L > g^P$. The longer the period, the larger the change in relative prices, and the larger the gap.

**Step 4: chain weighting.** The chain-weighted index takes the average of the two growth rates:

$$g^{\text{chain}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(g^L + g^P\right). \tag{6}$$

The statistical agencies use the **Fisher** index, which takes the geometric mean of the two growth factors instead, $1 + g^F = \sqrt{(1+g^L)(1+g^P)}$. When the two rates are close, the two averages are practically equal ([Appendix C.6](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.6-approximations)); the code below compares them.

**Step 5: linking the years into a chain.** Equation (6) is applied to every pair of neighboring years, so the weights are always the prices of those two years. To turn the growth rates into levels, pick a **benchmark year** $b$ in which real GDP is set equal to nominal GDP. Then move forward and backward one year at a time:

$$X_{t+1} = X_t\,(1 + g^{\text{chain}}_{t,t+1}), \qquad X_t = \frac{X_{t+1}}{1 + g^{\text{chain}}_{t,t+1}},$$

where $X_t$ is chained real GDP. Over several years the growth factors multiply, $X_T = X_b\,(1+g_{b,b+1})(1+g_{b+1,b+2})\cdots(1+g_{T-1,T})$. The levels are said to be in "chained year-$b$ dollars".

#### What the framework predicts

| From year $t$ to $t+1$ ... | Nominal GDP | Laspeyres $g^L$ | Paasche $g^P$ | Chained $g^{\text{chain}}$ | Price level $P$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| every price $\times\lambda$, same quantities | $\times\lambda$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | $\times\lambda$ |
| every quantity $\times\mu$, same prices | $\times\mu$ | $\mu-1$ | $\mu-1$ | $\mu-1$ | unchanged |
| relative prices change, same quantities | changes | 0 | 0 | 0 | moves with nominal GDP |
| quantities grow fastest where relative prices fall | rises | highest | lowest | in between | |

- **Real GDP ignores pure price changes.** When only prices move, every index reports zero real growth, and the whole change in nominal GDP shows up in the price level.
- **Fixed base years go out of date.** Over long spans the Laspeyres index overstates growth and the Paasche index understates it. The U.S. national accounts switched to chain weighting in the 1990s, when computer prices were falling fast.
- **Chained components do not add up.** Each chained component uses its own weights, so chained $C + I + G + NX$ generally differs from chained GDP. To compute **shares**, use nominal values, which do add up (equation 2). To compute **real growth rates**, use chained real values.

<!-- cell -->

### Price indexes and inflation

#### Definitions

- The **GDP deflator** is the price level of equation (4), $P_t = \text{nominal GDP}_t/\text{real GDP}_t$, usually multiplied by 100 so that it equals 100 in the base year.
- The **inflation rate** is the growth rate of the price level, $\pi_{t+1} \equiv P_{t+1}/P_t - 1$.
- Each quantity index has a matching **price index**. The Laspeyres price index values the *initial* quantities at both years' prices, $\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t}\big/\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t}$. The Paasche price index uses the *final* quantities, $\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t+1}\big/\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}$.

#### Deriving the results

**Step 1: nominal growth splits exactly into a price part and a quantity part.** Multiply and divide the growth factor of nominal GDP by $\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}$:

$$\frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t}} = \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}}}_{\text{Paasche price index}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t+1}}{\sum_i p_{i,t}q_{i,t}}}_{\text{Laspeyres quantity index}}.$$

Multiplying and dividing by $\sum_i p_{i,t+1}q_{i,t}$ instead gives the Laspeyres price index times the Paasche quantity index. Multiply the two splits and take the square root: the Fisher price index times the Fisher quantity index also equals the growth factor of nominal GDP, exactly. That is why a chained price index and chained real GDP always satisfy equation (4).

**Step 2: the growth rate of a product.** Write equation (4) in two neighboring years and divide. The growth factor of a product is the product of the growth factors:

$$1 + g_{\text{nominal}} = (1+\pi)(1+g_{\text{real}}) = 1 + \pi + g_{\text{real}} + \pi\,g_{\text{real}}.$$

Subtract 1 from both sides: $g_{\text{nominal}} = \pi + g_{\text{real}} + \pi\,g_{\text{real}}$. The last term is the product of two small numbers, so it is much smaller than the others, and ([Appendix C.5](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.5-growth-rates-and-the-growth-rules))

$$g_{\text{nominal GDP}} \approx \pi + g_{\text{real GDP}}. \tag{7}$$

To get inflation from the other two, solve the exact form for $\pi$: $\pi = (1+g_{\text{nominal}})/(1+g_{\text{real}}) - 1 \approx g_{\text{nominal}} - g_{\text{real}}$. With natural logs the split has no error at all: $\ln(\text{nominal GDP}) = \ln P + \ln(\text{real GDP})$, so the changes in logs add up exactly ([Appendix C.4](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.4-logarithms)).

*Intuition.* Nominal GDP can grow because each good costs more or because there are more goods. Equation (7) adds the two sources. The small cross term is the extra price increase on the extra goods.

**Step 3: rates over different periods.** With quarterly data, the change from a year ago compares a quarter with the same quarter one year earlier, $P_t/P_{t-4} - 1$. A one-quarter change is turned into an **annual rate** by compounding it four times, $(P_t/P_{t-1})^4 - 1$, which is close to four times the quarterly rate when that rate is small ([Appendix C.3](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.3-exponents-and-exponential-growth)). Over $T$ years, the **average annual growth rate** $\bar{g}$ is the constant rate that turns the first value into the last: $P_T = P_0(1+\bar{g})^T$. Raise both sides of $P_T/P_0 = (1+\bar{g})^T$ to the power $1/T$ and subtract 1:

$$\bar{g} = \left(\frac{P_T}{P_0}\right)^{1/T} - 1.$$

**Step 4: changing the base year.** Rebasing an index to year $b$ means $P'_t = 100 \times P_t/P_b$. The constant $100/P_b$ cancels in every ratio, $P'_{t+1}/P'_t = P_{t+1}/P_t$, so rebasing moves the level of the index but leaves every growth rate and inflation rate unchanged.

#### What the framework predicts

Taking the change in logs of equation (4), $\Delta\ln(\text{nominal GDP}) = \Delta\ln P + \Delta\ln(\text{real GDP})$: the **elasticity** of nominal GDP with respect to the price level is 1, and with respect to real GDP it is also 1.

| If ... | then ... |
|---|---|
| inflation is 1 point higher and real growth is unchanged | nominal growth is about 1 point higher |
| nominal growth is unchanged and real growth is 1 point higher | measured inflation is about 1 point lower |
| an index is rebased | its level changes; growth rates and inflation do not |

- **The rule of thumb in equation (7) is good when rates are small.** With 2 percent inflation and 2 percent real growth the cross term is only $0.02 \times 0.02 = 0.0004$, or 0.04 percentage points. In the apples-and-computers economy, with prices up 8 percent and quantities up 18 percent, it is about 1.5 points (see the checks below). In a high-inflation country it can be large.
- **Ratio scales show inflation directly.** Since $\ln P_t$ rises by about $\pi$ each year, a constant inflation rate is a straight line on a ratio (log) scale (Fig. 4).

<!-- cell -->

### Comparing countries: exchange rates and purchasing power parity

#### Definitions

We compare China with the United States; any pair of countries works the same way.

- The **exchange rate** $e$ is the number of yuan that buy one dollar in the currency market.
- China's GDP in its own currency is $Y^{\text{yuan}}$. Converted at the exchange rate, it is $\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}} = Y^{\text{yuan}}/e$.
- $\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}$ and $\text{price level}_{\text{China}}$ are what the same basket of goods costs in each country, both in dollars at the exchange rate. Their ratio, the **relative price level**, says how expensive China is compared with the United States.
- The **PPP conversion factor** is the number of yuan that buy in China what one dollar buys in the United States: $\text{PPP} = e \times \text{price level}_{\text{China}}/\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}$.

#### Deriving the results

**Step 1: China's real output.** Equation (4) holds in China too, with everything in dollars. Solving it for real GDP:

$$\text{real GDP}_{\text{China}} = \frac{\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}}.$$

**Step 2: value China's goods at U.S. prices.** For a fair comparison we value China's quantities at the prices that hold in the United States:

$$\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}} \times \text{real GDP}_{\text{China}}.$$

**Step 3: substitute Step 1 into Step 2.**

$$\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \frac{\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}} \times \text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}}. \tag{8}$$

Dollar GDP must be divided by China's relative price level. Where goods are cheap, the same dollars stand for more goods.

**Step 4: the shortcut through the PPP factor.** Put $\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}} = Y^{\text{yuan}}/e$ into (8) and collect the terms in the denominator:

$$\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \frac{Y^{\text{yuan}}}{e \times \text{price level}_{\text{China}}/\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}} = \frac{Y^{\text{yuan}}}{\text{PPP}}.$$

So we can skip the exchange rate altogether: dividing GDP in yuan by the PPP conversion factor gives GDP at U.S. prices.

**Step 5: how much of the gap is due to prices?** Divide (8) by U.S. GDP and take logs ([Appendix C.4](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/appC-math-review-for-macroeconomics.html#c.4-logarithms)):

$$\ln\frac{\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}}}{\text{GDP}_{\text{U.S.}}} = \ln\frac{\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}}}{\text{GDP}_{\text{U.S.}}} - \ln\frac{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}}.$$

The log gap at common prices equals the log gap at the exchange rate minus the log of the relative price level. If China is cheaper, that log is negative, and the gap at common prices is smaller. Dividing both GDPs by population gives the same split for GDP per person.

Valuing China's goods at U.S. prices is the cross-country version of a Laspeyres index; valuing U.S. goods at Chinese prices would be the Paasche version. In practice, the World Bank's International Comparison Program and the Penn World Table use average world prices ("international dollars"), much as chain weighting averages the two indexes over time.

#### What the framework predicts

| A 1% rise in ... | GDP at the exchange rate | GDP at common prices | Relative price level of China |
|---|---|---|---|
| the exchange rate $e$ (a weaker yuan), with yuan prices unchanged | $-1\%$ | 0 | $-1\%$ |
| every yuan price in China, with quantities unchanged | $+1\%$ | 0 | $+1\%$ |
| China's output of every good | $+1\%$ | $+1\%$ | 0 |

- **Common prices do not react to the currency market.** A swing in the exchange rate changes GDP in dollars one for one, but leaves the comparison at common prices untouched, because China's goods become cheaper in dollars by the same 1 percent (the elasticity of dollar GDP with respect to $e$ is $-1$).
- **Rich countries look less far ahead at common prices.** Services that cannot be traded, such as haircuts or restaurant meals, need a lot of labor, so they are cheap where wages are low. Poor countries therefore have low price levels, and comparisons at exchange rates exaggerate the income gaps between rich and poor countries.

<!-- cell -->

### The model in code

We now turn the measurement rules into Python functions, and then check every result above with numbers. Each function's description names the equation it computes.

> **Python note.** `def` creates a *function*: a named recipe that takes inputs (the *arguments*)
> and gives back a result with `return`. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what
> the function does. `.sum()` adds up all the values of a column or a row.

```{python}
def share(part, total):
    """Share of a part in a total, in percent (Tables 2.1 and 2.2; the shares of equation 2)."""
    return 100 * part / total


def gdp_value(prices, quantities):
    """Value of production: price times quantity, added over all goods (nominal or real GDP)."""
    return (prices * quantities).sum()


def chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche):
    """Chain-weighted growth: the average of the Laspeyres and Paasche growth rates (equation 6)."""
    return (g_laspeyres + g_paasche) / 2


def to_dollars(gdp_local, exchange_rate):
    """Convert GDP in local currency into dollars at the market exchange rate."""
    return gdp_local / exchange_rate


def at_common_prices(gdp_dollars, relative_price_level):
    """Real GDP at U.S. prices: dollar GDP divided by the price level relative to the U.S. (equation 8)."""
    return gdp_dollars / relative_price_level
```

**Check 1: value added adds up to final sales (equation 1).** A made-up chain of three producers: a farm
grows grain worth \$40 and sells it to a mill; the mill turns it into flour worth \$70 and sells it to a bakery;
the bakery sells bread worth \$120 to households.

> **Python note.** `pd.Series({...})` builds one labeled column from a dictionary: the keys become the
> labels. Subtracting two Series subtracts the values with the same label.

```{python}
revenue = pd.Series({"farm": 40, "mill": 70, "bakery": 120})
inputs = pd.Series({"farm": 0, "mill": 40, "bakery": 70})     # each buys the output of the one before
value_added = revenue - inputs
print(value_added)
print(f"Sum of value added:   ${value_added.sum()}")
print(f"Final sales (bread):  ${revenue['bakery']}")
print(f"Sum of all revenues:  ${revenue.sum()}   (counts the grain three times and the flour twice)")
```

**Check 2: the labor share (equation 3).** Take made-up round numbers for one year's income (in billions)
and check the algebra of Step 5: splitting proprietors' income in the economy-wide proportion gives the same
labor share as leaving it out of the fraction.

```{python}
gdi, taxes, proprietors, compensation = 100.0, 7.0, 9.0, 54.0
theta = compensation / (gdi - taxes - proprietors)                  # equation (3)
split = (compensation + theta * proprietors) / (gdi - taxes)        # proprietors' income split by theta
print(f"Labor share, equation (3):                 {theta:.4f}")
print(f"Labor share with proprietors split:        {split:.4f}")
print(f"Simple share, compensation / GDI:          {compensation / gdi:.4f}   (lower)")
```

**Check 3: real GDP in the economy of Table 2.4.** The textbook's example economy produces only apples
and computers. We store its prices and quantities in two small tables, one row per year.

> **Python note.** `pd.DataFrame({...}, index=[...])` builds a table from a dictionary: each key
> becomes a column and the `index` gives the row labels. `prices.loc[2026]` picks the row for 2026.
> Multiplying two rows, `prices.loc[2026] * quantities.loc[2027]`, multiplies the matching columns.

```{python}
prices = pd.DataFrame({"apples": [1, 2, 3], "computers": [900, 1000, 1000]}, index=[2025, 2026, 2027])
quantities = pd.DataFrame({"apples": [500, 500, 550], "computers": [5, 5, 6]}, index=[2025, 2026, 2027])
prices
```

Nominal GDP uses each year's own prices. Real GDP holds the prices fixed. The **Laspeyres** index
measures the change from 2026 to 2027 with the *initial* (2026) prices, and the **Paasche** index with
the *final* (2027) prices. **Chain weighting** averages the two growth rates (equation 6).

> **Python note.** An *f-string* such as `f"{x:,.0f}"` inserts the value of a variable into a piece
> of text: `,` adds thousands separators, `.0f` shows no decimals and `.1%` shows a share as a
> percentage with one decimal.

```{python}
for year in [2025, 2026, 2027]:
    print(f"Nominal GDP in {year}: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[year], quantities.loc[year]):,.0f}")

g_nominal = gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
g_laspeyres = gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
g_paasche = gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2027]) / gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2026]) - 1
g_chain = chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche)
print(f"Real GDP in 2027 at 2026 prices: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2027]):,.0f}")
print(f"Real GDP in 2026 at 2027 prices: ${gdp_value(prices.loc[2027], quantities.loc[2026]):,.0f}")
print(f"Growth 2026-2027: nominal {g_nominal:.1%}, Laspeyres {g_laspeyres:.1%}, "
      f"Paasche {g_paasche:.1%}, chain-weighted {g_chain:.1%}")
print(f"Chained real GDP in 2026, benchmarked to 2027: ${7650 / (1 + g_chain):,.0f}")
print(f"Inflation (nominal growth minus real growth):  {g_nominal - g_chain:.1%}")
```

These are the numbers of Table 2.4: real growth is 18.3 percent at 2026 prices, 17.7 percent at
2027 prices, and 18.0 percent chain-weighted. Nominal GDP grew 27.5 percent, so by the rule of thumb in
equation (7) prices rose by about $27.5 - 18.0 = 9.5$ percent. (The textbook gets \$6,483 for chained real
GDP in 2026, because it rounds the growth rate to 18.0 percent first; with the unrounded rate we get \$6,482.)

**Check 4: the two indexes as weighted averages (equation 5).** Apples grew 10 percent and computers 20
percent. Weighting these rates with the 2026 spending shares must give the Laspeyres rate, and the harmonic
form with the 2027 shares must give the Paasche rate. If every price rises by the same factor, the two
indexes must agree.

```{python}
p0, p1 = prices.loc[2026], prices.loc[2027]
q0, q1 = quantities.loc[2026], quantities.loc[2027]
s0 = p0 * q0 / gdp_value(p0, q0)                 # spending shares in 2026
s1 = p1 * q1 / gdp_value(p1, q1)                 # spending shares in 2027
growth_i = q1 / q0 - 1                           # growth of each good's quantity
print(f"Shares of computers: {s0['computers']:.3f} in 2026, {s1['computers']:.3f} in 2027")
print(f"Laspeyres: direct {g_laspeyres:.4%}   share-weighted average {(s0 * growth_i).sum():.4%}")
print(f"Paasche:   direct {g_paasche:.4%}   harmonic form          {1 / (s1 / (1 + growth_i)).sum() - 1:.4%}")
p_scaled = 1.5 * p0                              # every price 50% higher: relative prices unchanged
g_scaled = gdp_value(p_scaled, q1) / gdp_value(p_scaled, q0) - 1
print(f"Paasche when all prices rise by the same factor: {g_scaled:.4%} (= Laspeyres)")
```

The price of apples rose by half while computers kept their price, so computers became relatively cheaper,
and their quantity grew faster. At the 2026 prices computers carry more weight, which is why the
Laspeyres rate is the higher one.

**Check 5: the exact split of nominal growth, and the Fisher index.** Step 1 of the price block says that a
price index times the matching quantity index gives the growth factor of nominal GDP exactly. Step 2 says
that the rule of thumb in equation (7) misses the cross term $\pi\,g$.

> **Python note.** `x ** 0.5` is the square root of `x`.

```{python}
price_laspeyres = gdp_value(p1, q0) / gdp_value(p0, q0)
price_paasche = gdp_value(p1, q1) / gdp_value(p0, q1)
price_fisher = (price_laspeyres * price_paasche) ** 0.5
g_fisher = ((1 + g_laspeyres) * (1 + g_paasche)) ** 0.5 - 1
print(f"Nominal growth factor:                     {1 + g_nominal:.5f}")
print(f"Paasche price x Laspeyres quantity:        {price_paasche * (1 + g_laspeyres):.5f}")
print(f"Laspeyres price x Paasche quantity:        {price_laspeyres * (1 + g_paasche):.5f}")
print(f"Fisher price x Fisher quantity:            {price_fisher * (1 + g_fisher):.5f}")
print(f"Real growth: chain-weighted {g_chain:.4%}, Fisher {g_fisher:.4%}")
exact = (1 + g_nominal) / (1 + g_chain) - 1
print(f"Inflation: rule of thumb {g_nominal - g_chain:.2%}, exact {exact:.2%}, "
      f"Fisher price index {price_fisher - 1:.2%}")
print(f"Cross term pi x g: {exact * g_chain:.2%}  ->  {exact:.2%} + {g_chain:.2%} + {exact * g_chain:.2%} "
      f"= {exact + g_chain + exact * g_chain:.2%}")
```

The four products agree to the last digit, and the arithmetic and geometric averages of the two growth
rates differ only in the third decimal. But with rates this large, the rule of thumb is off: prices in this
economy rose by about 8.0 percent, not 9.5. The missing 1.5 points are the cross term.

**Check 6: rates over different periods.** A price level that rises 1 percent every quarter rises by more
than 4 percent a year, because the increases compound. And a price level that doubles in 10 years grows at
an average annual rate of $2^{1/10} - 1$.

```{python}
quarterly = 0.01
print(f"1% a quarter, compounded: {(1 + quarterly) ** 4 - 1:.4%} a year (simple rule: {4 * quarterly:.0%})")
g_bar = 2 ** (1 / 10) - 1
print(f"Prices double in 10 years: average growth {g_bar:.3%} a year")
print(f"Check: (1 + {g_bar:.5f})^10 = {(1 + g_bar) ** 10:.4f}")
```

**Check 7: China and the United States at common prices (equation 8).** We use the textbook's 2019 numbers:
U.S. GDP of \$20.6 trillion, China's GDP of 95.1 trillion yuan, 6.91 yuan per dollar, and Chinese prices at
68.4 percent of U.S. prices.

```{python}
china_dollars = to_dollars(95.1, 6.91)                  # 95.1 trillion yuan, 6.91 yuan per dollar (2019)
china_ppp = at_common_prices(china_dollars, 0.684)      # goods in China cost 68.4% of U.S. prices
print(f"China at the exchange rate: ${china_dollars:.1f} trillion, {china_dollars / 20.6:.0%} of U.S. GDP")
print(f"China at common prices:     ${china_ppp:.1f} trillion, {china_ppp / 20.6:.0%} of U.S. GDP")
```

With these numbers, China's economy looks like two-thirds of the U.S. economy at the exchange rate, but
almost exactly as large at common prices. The next cell checks Steps 4 and 5 and the first row of the table
of predictions: the PPP shortcut, the log split of the gap, and a 1 percent weaker yuan.

> **Python note.** `np.log` is the natural logarithm.

```{python}
ppp = 6.91 * 0.684                                      # yuan that buy what one dollar buys in the U.S.
print(f"PPP factor: {ppp:.3f} yuan per dollar; 95.1 / PPP = ${95.1 / ppp:.2f} trillion (= {china_ppp:.2f})")
gap_exchange, gap_prices = np.log(china_dollars / 20.6), np.log(0.684)
print(f"Log gap at the exchange rate {gap_exchange:.4f} - log relative price level {gap_prices:.4f} "
      f"= {gap_exchange - gap_prices:.4f};  log gap at common prices {np.log(china_ppp / 20.6):.4f}")
e_new = 6.91 * 1.01                                     # the yuan weakens by 1 percent
dollars_new = to_dollars(95.1, e_new)
ppp_new = at_common_prices(dollars_new, ppp / e_new)    # China's relative price level falls with e
print(f"1% weaker yuan: GDP in dollars {dollars_new / china_dollars - 1:+.2%}, "
      f"at common prices {ppp_new / china_ppp - 1:+.2%}")
```

The log gap at common prices is close to zero, so China and the United States had almost the same GDP. A
weaker yuan makes China's GDP look about 1 percent smaller in dollars, while the comparison at common prices
does not move at all.

## Who buys GDP: the expenditure side

We first split GDP into consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports, and follow the shares of the four parts over time.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 1: Composition of U.S. GDP

**Goal.** See how the four spending shares of U.S. GDP have moved since 1929.

The file has one row per year and one column per share of GDP, in percent.

```{python}
shares = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig2-1.csv")
shares.tail()
```

The national income identity, equation (2), says the four shares must add up to 100 percent in every year. Let us check.

```{python}
total = shares.consumption_share + shares.investment_share + shares.government_share + shares.net_exports_share
print(f"C + I + G + NX, as a percent of GDP: between {total.min():.2f} and {total.max():.2f}")
```

The table is **wide**: one column per component. Plotly Express prefers **long** tables, with one row
per component and year.

> **Python note.** `.melt(id_vars="year")` turns the share columns into rows: the old column names go
> into a new column (`var_name`) and the numbers into another (`value_name`). `.map(NAMES)` then replaces
> each column name with a readable name, using the dictionary `NAMES`.

```{python}
NAMES = {"net_exports_share": "Net exports", "consumption_share": "Consumption",
         "investment_share": "Investment", "government_share": "Government purchases"}
long = shares.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="series", value_name="share")
long["component"] = long.series.map(NAMES)
long.head()
```

<!-- cell -->

#### The same accounts for other countries

The World Bank publishes the same four shares for about 190 countries, in `expenditure_world.csv`
(from 1960 for many). A second file, `countries.csv`, lists every economy with its world region and its
membership of the G7, the G20 and the OECD; the website's country menus use it.

```{python}
world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "expenditure_world.csv")
countries = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
world[world.country == "China"].tail(3)
```

The World Bank follows the United Nations' *System of National Accounts*, which draws one line
differently from the BEA: what governments spend on roads, buildings and equipment counts as
**investment**, and government purchases cover only government *consumption*. Compare the U.S. numbers
of the two sources.

> **Python note.** `pd.DataFrame({...})` builds a table from several columns; their rows are matched by
> year. `.loc[[1970, 2000, 2024]]` keeps three years.

```{python}
bea = shares.set_index("year")
wb = world[world.country == "United States"].set_index("year")
pd.DataFrame({"I, BEA": bea.investment_share, "I, World Bank": wb.investment,
              "G, BEA": bea.government_share, "G, World Bank": wb.government}).loc[[1970, 2000, 2024]].round(1)
```

The World Bank's investment share is about 4 points higher and its government share about 4 points
lower: the same spending sits in a different box. Consumption and net exports agree. **Before you compare
countries, check that the numbers use the same definitions.**

The textbook stacks the shares on top of each other: net exports at the bottom, then consumption,
investment, and government purchases up to 100 percent. `px.area` stacks areas in the order of
`category_orders`, and `color_discrete_map` gives each component a fixed color. Because net exports are
negative in recent decades, consumption starts *below* zero in those years. The function draws the BEA's
U.S. data, or the World Bank's data for any other country.

> **Python note.** `np.floor` and `np.ceil` round down and up, so `10 * np.ceil(x / 10)` is the next
> multiple of 10 above `x`: the axes grow in steps of 10 points for countries with unusual shares.
> `data.groupby("year").share.sum()` adds up the four shares within each year (the top of the stack),
> and `max(a, b)` is the larger of two numbers.

```{python}
ORDER = ["Net exports", "Consumption", "Investment", "Government purchases"]
COLORS_GDP = {"Net exports": "#e0a33b", "Consumption": "#5aa0d8", "Investment": GREEN, "Government purchases": TEAL}
LABELS = {"year": "Year", "share": "Percent of GDP", "component": "Component"}
WB_NAMES = {"consumption": "Consumption", "investment": "Investment", "government": "Government purchases",
            "net_exports": "Net exports"}
BEA = "United States (BEA)"


def composition_chart(style="stacked areas", country=BEA):
    """Fig. 2.1: the expenditure shares of GDP, stacked or as separate lines (BEA, or World Bank data)."""
    data = long
    title = "Since 1950: consumption ≈ 64%, government ≈ 20%, investment ≈ 17% of U.S. GDP"
    if country != BEA:
        data = world[world.country == country].melt(id_vars="year", value_vars=list(WB_NAMES), value_name="share")
        data["component"] = data.variable.map(WB_NAMES)
        title = f"Composition of GDP in {country} (World Bank definitions)"
    if style == "stacked areas":
        fig = px.area(data, x="year", y="share", color="component", color_discrete_map=COLORS_GDP,
                      category_orders={"component": ORDER}, labels=LABELS, title=title)
    else:
        fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="share", color="component", color_discrete_map=COLORS_GDP,
                      category_orders={"component": ORDER}, labels=LABELS, title=title)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    top = max(data.groupby("year").share.sum().max(), data.share.max())     # stacked total or largest share
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[data.year.min(), 2025])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[min(-10, 10 * np.floor(data.share.min() / 10)), max(100, 10 * np.ceil(top / 10))])
    return fig
```

> **Python note.** `interact` draws the figure again whenever you change a widget. `ToggleButtons`
> is a row of buttons, one per option, and a `Dropdown` is a menu from which you choose one entry. The `;`
> at the end only hides an extra line of text.

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(composition_chart,
         style=ToggleButtons(options=["stacked areas", "separate lines"], description="chart", style=WIDE),
         country=Dropdown(options=[BEA] + sorted(world.country.unique()), value=BEA, description="country"));
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: Fig. 1 with buttons for the chart style and a menu of countries (G20 and OECD)
members = countries[countries.g20 | countries.oecd].country
fig = dropdown_figure(composition_chart, "country", [BEA] + sorted(set(members) & set(world.country)), start=BEA)
fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [dict(type="buttons", direction="right", x=0, xanchor="left",
    y=1.02, yanchor="bottom", buttons=[dict(label="stacked areas", method="restyle", args=[{"stackgroup": "1"}]),
```

**What to notice.**

- From 1950 on, the shares hardly move: consumption averages about 64 percent, government purchases
  about 20 percent and investment about 17 percent (see the numbers below).
- World War II stands out. In 1943–1944 government purchases took 48 percent of GDP, and consumption
  and investment were squeezed.
- During the Great Depression, investment collapsed to 3 percent of GDP in 1932, while the
  consumption share peaked at 82 percent.
- Net exports were zero or slightly positive for most years before 1976, and negative in every year
  since. The deficit was deepest in 2006. Hover over the lines to read the values, and click a
  component in the legend to hide it.
- Choose China: in 2024 consumption was only 40 percent of GDP and investment also 40 percent, about
  twice the U.S. investment share. Choose Ireland: in 2025 its net exports were 40 percent of GDP,
  because multinational firms book large exports there.

> **Python note.** `.set_index("year")` uses the years as row labels, so `by_year.loc[1950:]` keeps the
> rows from 1950 on. `.idxmax()` returns the row label (here the year) of the largest value, and
> `.idxmin()` that of the smallest.

```{python}
by_year = shares.set_index("year")
print("Average shares, 1950-2025 (percent):")
print(by_year.loc[1950:].mean().round(1))
print(f"Government purchases peaked at {by_year.government_share.max():.1f}% in {by_year.government_share.idxmax()}")
print(f"Investment fell to {by_year.investment_share.min():.1f}% in {by_year.investment_share.idxmin()}")
print(f"Deepest trade deficit: {by_year.net_exports_share.min():.1f}% in {by_year.net_exports_share.idxmin()}")
print(f"Last year with a trade surplus: {by_year[by_year.net_exports_share > 0].index.max()}")
```

#### Key numbers: Table 2.1, the expenditure approach

The textbook's Table 2.1 breaks down U.S. GDP in 2022 in more detail. A wider data file holds the
national accounts lines behind it, in billions of current dollars, for every year since 1929.

```{python}
nipa = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "nipa_annual.csv").set_index("year")
nipa.loc[2022]
```

The function below builds the table for any year. Population is in thousands, so GDP per person in
dollars is billions × 1,000,000 / population.

```{python}
EXPENDITURE = {"gdp": "Gross domestic product", "consumption": "Personal consumption expenditures",
               "motor_vehicles": "   Motor vehicles and parts", "food": "   Food", "housing": "   Housing",
               "medical": "   Medical care", "investment": "Gross private domestic investment",
               "structures": "   Structures (nonresidential)", "equipment": "   Equipment",
               "ipp": "   Intellectual property products", "residential": "   Residential",
               "government": "Government purchases", "defense": "   National defense",
               "net_exports": "Net exports of goods and services", "exports": "   Exports", "imports": "   Imports"}


def expenditure_table(year):
    """Table 2.1: the expenditure approach to U.S. GDP in one year."""
    row = nipa.loc[year, list(EXPENDITURE)]
    table = pd.DataFrame({"Trillions of dollars": row / 1000,
                          "Share of GDP (percent)": share(row, row["gdp"]),
                          "Per person (dollars)": row * 1_000_000 / nipa.loc[year, "population"]})
    table.index = list(EXPENDITURE.values())
    return table.round(1)
```

We put the textbook's shares next to ours, to compare.

```{python}
table_2022 = expenditure_table(2022)
table_2022["Textbook share"] = [100.0, 68.2, 2.7, 5.1, 11.8, 10.6, 18.0, 2.4, 5.1, 5.5, 4.3, 17.3, 3.5, -3.9, 11.8, 15.7]
table_2022
```

```{python}
gdp_2022 = nipa.loc[2022, "gdp"] / 1000
print(f"GDP in 2022: ${gdp_2022:.2f} trillion in our data, $25.5 trillion in the textbook "
      f"({gdp_2022 / 25.5 - 1:.1%} higher)")
```

Our numbers are close to the textbook's but not identical. This is a lesson about data: **national
accounts are revised**. In 2023 the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) did a comprehensive update
that raised the level of U.S. GDP in 2022 by about 2 percent, after the textbook's numbers were
collected. Shares change much less than levels: consumption is still about 68 percent of GDP,
investment about 18–19 percent and government purchases about 17 percent.

### Fig. 2: Expenditure shares of U.S. GDP

**Goal.** Zoom in on the years since 1970, when the consumption share started to rise.

```{python}
recent = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig2-2.csv")
recent = recent.rename(columns={"consumption_share": "Consumption", "investment_share": "Investment",
                                "government_share": "Government purchases", "net_exports_share": "Net exports"})
recent.head()
```

As in the textbook, consumption is measured on its own axis on the right, because it is much larger
than the other three shares. The function draws the BEA's U.S. data, or the World Bank's data (from
1970) for any other country; both axes widen in steps of 10 points when a country's shares do not fit.

> **Python note.** `px.line` with a list of columns as `y` draws one line per column. We then add the
> consumption line with `fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(...))`, and `yaxis="y2"` attaches it to a second
> vertical axis. In `update_layout`, `overlaying="y"` puts that axis on top of the first one, and
> `side="right"` puts its labels on the right. `.rename(columns=WB_NAMES)` gives the World Bank's
> columns the same names as ours, `data.iloc[0]` is the first row and `data.iloc[-1]` the last, and
> `"rose" if a > b else "fell"` picks one of two words.

```{python}
def shares_chart(country=BEA):
    """Fig. 2.2: expenditure shares since 1970, consumption on the right axis (BEA, or World Bank data)."""
    data = recent
    if country != BEA:
        data = world[(world.country == country) & (world.year >= 1970)].rename(columns=WB_NAMES)
    first, last = data.iloc[0], data.iloc[-1]
    verb = "rose" if last.Consumption > first.Consumption else "fell"
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y=["Government purchases", "Investment", "Net exports"],
                  color_discrete_sequence=[TEAL, GREEN, "#e0a33b"],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Share of GDP (percent)", "variable": "Component"},
                  title=f"{country}: consumption {verb} from {first.Consumption:.0f}% to {last.Consumption:.0f}% "
                        f"of GDP, {first.year:.0f}–{last.year:.0f}")
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=data.year, y=data.Consumption, name="Consumption (right axis)",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), yaxis="y2"))
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    others = data[["Government purchases", "Investment", "Net exports"]]
    low, high = min(-6, 10 * np.floor(others.min().min() / 10)), max(46, 10 * np.ceil(others.max().max() / 10) + 20)
    c_low, c_high = min(36, 10 * np.floor(data.Consumption.min() / 10) - 30), max(70, 10 * np.ceil(data.Consumption.max() / 10))
    fig.update_layout(yaxis=dict(range=[low, high], tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25] if high == 46 else None),
                      yaxis2=dict(title="Consumption (percent of GDP)", overlaying="y", side="right",
                                  range=[c_low, c_high], tickvals=[60, 64, 68] if c_low == 36 else None, showgrid=False),
                      legend=dict(x=1.1), xaxis=dict(range=[1969, 2026]))      # legend clear of the right axis
    return fig
```


```{python}
wide = recent.set_index("year")
pd.DataFrame({"1970": wide.loc[1970], "2025": wide.loc[2025], "change": wide.loc[2025] - wide.loc[1970]}).round(1)
```

The consumption share rose from 60.3 percent in 1970 to 67.6 percent in 2025, and since 2010 it has
stayed between about 66.6 and 68.6 percent. The government share fell from 23.5 to 17.4 percent, and
net exports went from a small surplus to a deficit of 3.0 percent. Because the four shares always add
up to 100, **the four changes must add up to zero**: a rise in one share is always matched by falls in
others. The chart below shows the changes directly.

> **Python note.** `wide.loc[base_year:] - wide.loc[base_year]` subtracts one row from every row of the
> table, column by column. The result is the change of each share since the base year, in percentage points.
> `.reset_index()` turns the year labels back into an ordinary column, which `melt` and Plotly need.

```{python}
CHANGE_COLORS = {"Consumption": BLUE, "Investment": GREEN, "Government purchases": TEAL, "Net exports": "#e0a33b"}


def changes_chart(base_year=1970):
    """Fig. 2.2, second view: change in each expenditure share since base_year (percentage points)."""
    changes = (wide.loc[base_year:] - wide.loc[base_year]).reset_index()
    long_changes = changes.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="component", value_name="change")
    fig = px.line(long_changes, x="year", y="change", color="component", color_discrete_map=CHANGE_COLORS,
                  range_x=[1970, 2025], range_y=[-8, 10],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "change": f"Change since {base_year} (percentage points)",
                          "component": "Component"})
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black", line_width=1)
    c = wide.loc[2025] - wide.loc[base_year]
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{base_year}–2025: C {c['Consumption']:+.1f}, I {c['Investment']:+.1f}, "
                            f"G {c['Government purchases']:+.1f}, NX {c['Net exports']:+.1f} points")
    return fig
```

> **Python note.** A `Dropdown` is a menu of choices. Here it lists the possible base years.

## Who earns GDP: labor's share

The same GDP is also income. Here we ask how much of it goes to workers, and whether that share has really stayed constant.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 3: Labor's share of GDP

**Goal.** Check one of the classic "stylized facts" of macroeconomics: that labor earns about
two-thirds of GDP, year after year.

The income approach splits GDP into the income earned by workers (**compensation**: wages, salaries
and benefits) and the income earned by the owners of capital. Two parts need care. Taxes on
production (such as sales taxes) are income of neither, so they are left out. And the income of
the self-employed (**proprietors' income**) mixes both, so it is split between labor and capital in
the same proportion as in the rest of the economy. The result is

$$\text{labor share} = \frac{\text{compensation}}{\text{GDI} - \text{taxes on production} - \text{proprietors' income}}$$

where GDI is gross domestic income, the income-side measure of GDP.

```{python}
labor = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig2-3.csv")
labor.tail()
```

We can rebuild this measure from the national accounts lines in `nipa`.

```{python}
rebuilt = nipa.compensation / (nipa.gdi - nipa.taxes_less_subsidies - nipa.proprietors_income)
print(f"Labor share in 2022: {rebuilt[2022]:.4f} rebuilt from nipa, "
      f"{labor[labor.year == 2022].labor_share.iloc[0]:.4f} in the figure file")
```

The labor share is a classic cross-country fact too. The Penn World Table, a database of national
accounts for about 180 countries, estimates it for 140 of them from 1950 on (`labor_share_world.csv`).
Its method differs a little from the textbook's: it treats the income of the self-employed in other
ways, depending on the data each country has. For the United States its share is about 0.03 lower.

```{python}
pwt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "labor_share_world.csv")
us_pwt = pwt[pwt.country == "United States"].set_index("year").labor_share
print(f"{pwt.country.nunique()} countries, {pwt.year.min()}-{pwt.year.max()}")
print(f"U.S. 2019: {us_pwt[2019]:.3f} in the Penn World Table, {labor.set_index('year').labor_share[2019]:.3f} in Fig. 3")
```

Each country keeps one color in every chart: a few have fixed colors, and the others take one of 24
distinct colors in turn.

> **Python note.** `for i, name in enumerate(...)` hands over each name together with its position `i`
> (0, 1, 2, ...). `i % 24` is the remainder after dividing by 24, so the 24 colors repeat in turn.
> `if name not in COLORS:` skips the names that already have a color.

```{python}
COLORS = {"United States": BLUE, "Germany": TEAL, "Japan": GREEN, "China": "#e0a33b", "United Kingdom": "#5aa0d8"}
OTHER = px.colors.qualitative.Dark24                 # 24 distinct colors for the other countries
for i, name in enumerate(countries.country):
    if name not in COLORS:
        COLORS[name] = OTHER[i % len(OTHER)]
```

The textbook points to a downward trend since about 1970. Our chart adds a straight trend line fitted to
the data: pick the year where the line starts, and see how steep the decline is. You can also add other countries from the Penn World Table
(including the United States, to compare the two measures).

> **Python note.** `np.polyfit(x, y, 1)` fits the best straight line $y = a + bx$ through the points
> (by least squares) and returns the slope $b$ first and the intercept $a$ second. `SelectMultiple` is a
> list from which you can pick several entries: hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click to add or remove one.
> `.isin(chosen)` keeps the rows of the chosen countries, and `for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):`
> hands over each country's name and rows in turn, so each gets its own line. `pd.concat([a, b])` stacks
> two columns into one, and `x if condition else y` picks `x` when the condition is true.

```{python}
def labor_share_chart(start=1970, chosen=()):
    """Fig. 2.3: labor's share of GDP, 1950-2025, with a trend line from `start`; other countries from PWT."""
    after = labor[labor.year >= start]
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(after.year, after.labor_share, 1)
    fig = px.line(labor, x="year", y="labor_share", labels={"year": "Year", "labor_share": "Labor share of GDP"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), fill="tozeroy", fillcolor="rgba(22, 82, 140, 0.12)",
                      name="Labor share (textbook)", showlegend=True)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=after.year, y=intercept + slope * after.year, name=f"Trend since {start}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    extra = pwt[pwt.country.isin(chosen)]
    for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.year, y=part.labor_share, name=f"{name} (PWT)", line=dict(color=COLORS[name])))
    shown = pd.concat([labor.labor_share, extra.labor_share])      # every value on the chart
    low = 0.55 if shown.min() >= 0.55 else 0.05 * np.floor(shown.min() / 0.05)      # widen in steps of 0.05
    high = 0.75 if shown.max() <= 0.75 else 0.05 * np.ceil(shown.max() / 0.05)
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1950, 2025])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[low, high], tickvals=[0.6, 0.65, 0.7, 0.75] if low == 0.55 else None)  # no corner label
    # slope is per year, as a fraction: x 100 for percentage points, x 10 for a decade
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Labor share: trend since {start} is {1000 * slope:+.1f} percentage points per decade")
    return fig
```

```{python}
         start=Dropdown(options=[1950, 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000], value=1970, description="trend from",
                        style=WIDE),
         chosen=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(pwt.country.unique()), value=(), rows=8, description="add (PWT)"));
```


[taxes on production and imports less subsidies (`W254RC1A027NBEA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/W254RC1A027NBEA) and [proprietors’ income (`A041RC1A027NBEA`)](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/A041RC1A027NBEA);
other countries: [Penn World Table 11.0, labor share (`labsh`), Groningen Growth and Development Centre](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/)
(Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015, [doi:10.34894/FABVLR](https://doi.org/10.34894/FABVLR)). Country groups: [World Bank country classifications](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups).

(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch02/README.md)).

<!-- cell -->

On the website, the menu above the chart adds a group of countries from the Penn World Table; click a
country in the legend to hide it.

```{python}
share_by_year = labor.set_index("year").labor_share
print(f"Average 1950-2025: {share_by_year.mean():.3f}")
print(f"Highest: {share_by_year.max():.3f} in {share_by_year.idxmax()}; lowest: {share_by_year.min():.3f} in {share_by_year.idxmin()}")
print(f"Average 1950-1969: {share_by_year.loc[1950:1969].mean():.3f}; average 2010-2025: {share_by_year.loc[2010:].mean():.3f}")
print("Years below 0.60:", list(share_by_year[share_by_year < 0.60].index))
```

**What to notice.**

- On average, labor earned 0.65 of income from 1950 to 2025, close to the two-thirds of the stylized
  fact. Until 2021 the share stayed between 0.60 and 0.70.
- But the share is not constant. It peaked at 0.69 in 1970 and has drifted down since: from 1970 the
  trend falls by about 1.3 percentage points per decade. Move the starting year to 1990 or 2000 and
  the decline looks even steeper.
- Since 2022 the share has been below 0.60 for the first time in these data (0.586 in 2025). Our values
  for the last years in the textbook are slightly lower than the book's, because of the 2023 data
  revision. Part of the decline reflects how the national accounts treat software and R&D, which is
  still debated by researchers.
- Add other countries. The labor share fell in Germany too (0.69 in 1970, 0.64 in 2023), but it rose in
  Japan (0.51 to 0.59) and South Korea (0.42 to 0.55). Two-thirds is a rough rule for rich countries,
  not a law of nature. Oil exporters such as Qatar (0.18) and Kuwait (0.25) have very low shares,
  because most of their income is oil revenue. Some values are doubtful: the Penn World Table puts
  Venezuela at exactly 0.0844 in every year from 2019 to 2023, a value carried forward, not measured. **Look at the extremes before you trust
  a cross-country file.**

#### Key numbers: Table 2.2, the income approach

```{python}
INCOME = {"gdp": "Gross domestic product", "compensation": "Compensation of employees",
          "wages": "   Wages and salaries", "benefits": "   Benefits",
          "taxes_less_subsidies": "Taxes less subsidies on businesses",
          "net_operating_surplus": "Net operating surplus of businesses",
          "depreciation": "Depreciation of fixed capital"}


def income_table(year):
    """Table 2.2: the income approach to U.S. GDP in one year."""
    row = nipa.loc[year, list(INCOME)]
    table = pd.DataFrame({"Trillions of dollars": row / 1000,
                          "Share of GDP (percent)": share(row, row["gdp"]),
                          "Per person (dollars)": row * 1_000_000 / nipa.loc[year, "population"]})
    table.index = list(INCOME.values())
    return table.round(1)


income_2022 = income_table(2022)
income_2022["Textbook share"] = [100.0, 53.2, 43.9, 9.3, 6.5, 23.5, 16.8]
income_2022
```

Compensation, taxes, the operating surplus and depreciation should add up to total income. They do,
but to **gross domestic income** (GDI) rather than to GDP. The two differ by a small *statistical
discrepancy*, because the BEA measures spending and income from different sources.

```{python}
y = nipa.loc[2022]
income_sum = y.compensation + y.taxes_less_subsidies + y.net_operating_surplus + y.depreciation
print(f"Sum of the income lines: {income_sum:,.0f} billion")
print(f"GDI: {y.gdi:,.0f} billion;  GDP: {y.gdp:,.0f} billion;  gap: {share(y.gdi - y.gdp, y.gdp):.2f}% of GDP")
```

In the current data, compensation is 51.6 percent of GDP in 2022, below the textbook's 53.2 percent:
the 2023 revision raised the operating surplus of businesses by about half a trillion dollars.
Depreciation, the wear and tear of capital, is about 16.5 percent of GDP.

**A note on Table 2.3 (Beyond GDP).** The textbook reports Jones and Klenow's welfare measure, which
adds life expectancy, leisure and consumption inequality to consumption per person. It shows that
Western Europe is closer to the United States than GDP suggests, and most poor countries further
away. The measure needs household-survey data on consumption inequality that are not openly
available, so we do not rebuild it here.

## Prices and inflation

Nominal GDP rises when prices rise and when production rises. These figures pull out the price part: the price level and its growth rate, inflation.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 4: The level of the GDP deflator

**Goal.** Follow the U.S. price level since 1947, as measured by the **GDP deflator**.

The GDP deflator is the price level in equation (4): nominal GDP divided by real GDP. It is an
**index**: its value in a chosen base year is set to 100. The data are quarterly, with one row per
quarter labeled by the first day of the quarter.

> **Python note.** `parse_dates=["date"]` tells pandas that the `date` column holds dates, not plain
> text. Plotly then draws a proper time axis, and we can pick rows by year.

```{python}
deflator = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig2-4.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv")
deflator.tail()
```

FRED shades the recessions in gray. The file `recessions.csv` lists the first and last month of each
recession since 1947, as dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER).

> **Python note.** `range(len(recessions))` gives the row numbers 0, 1, 2, …, so the `for` loop visits
> every recession once. `fig.add_vrect` draws a vertical band between two dates.

```{python}
def shade_recessions(fig):
    """Add a gray band for every NBER recession, as FRED does (Figs. 2.4 and 2.5)."""
    for i in range(len(recessions)):
        fig.add_vrect(x0=recessions.start[i], x1=recessions.end[i], fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.25, line_width=0)
    return fig
```

The World Bank publishes the GDP deflator of about 200 countries, once a year. Each country publishes
its index with its own base year, so `deflator_world.csv` has been **rebased**: every country's deflator
is divided by its 2012 value and multiplied by 100, like the U.S. series. The file also holds the
yearly inflation rate of each deflator, which Fig. 5 uses. We place each yearly value in the middle of
its year.

> **Python note.** `.astype(str)` turns numbers into text, so `deflators.year.astype(str) + "-07-01"`
> builds dates such as `"2012-07-01"`, and `pd.to_datetime` turns that text into real dates.

```{python}
deflators = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "deflator_world.csv")
deflators["date"] = pd.to_datetime(deflators.year.astype(str) + "-07-01")   # mid-year
print("Every country's deflator in 2012:", deflators[deflators.year == 2012].deflator_2012_100.dropna().unique())
deflators[deflators.country == "Japan"].tail(3)
```

The chart draws the U.S. quarterly series and, if you choose them, other countries' yearly series. When a
chosen country's prices were far lower or higher, the axis widens tenfold until every value fits.

> **Python note.** A `while` loop repeats its indented lines as long as its condition is true: here it
> multiplies the top of the axis by 10 until the largest value fits below it (and divides the bottom of
> the ratio scale by 10 until the smallest value fits above it).

```{python}
def deflator_chart(scale="linear", chosen=()):
    """Fig. 2.4: the GDP deflator (2012 = 100), U.S. quarterly since 1947, other countries yearly."""
    fig = px.line(deflator, x="date", y="gdp_deflator_2012_100", log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
                  labels={"date": "Quarter", "gdp_deflator_2012_100": "GDP deflator (index, 2012 = 100)"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), name="United States (quarterly)", showlegend=True)
    extra = deflators[deflators.country.isin(chosen)].dropna(subset=["deflator_2012_100"])
    for name, part in extra.groupby("country"):
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=part.date, y=part.deflator_2012_100, name=name, line=dict(color=COLORS[name])))
    shade_recessions(fig)
    shown = pd.concat([deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100, extra.deflator_2012_100])
    low, high = 9, (170 if scale == "ratio" else 150)
    while low > shown.min():
        low = low / 10                   # widen the axis tenfold at a time until every value fits
    while high < shown.max():
        high = high * 10
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[10, 20, 40, 80, 160] if (low, high) == (9, 170) else None,
                         range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high])
    factor = deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100.iloc[-1] / deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100.iloc[0]
    fig.update_layout(title=f"The U.S. price level rose about {factor:.0f}-fold from 1947 to 2026")
    return fig
```

```{python}
                               rows=8, description="add countries"));
```

```{python}
    dict(label="linear scale", method="relayout", args=[{"yaxis.type": "linear", "yaxis.autorange": True}]),
```

On the website, the menu above the chart adds a group of countries (yearly data); the buttons switch the
scale. Use the ratio scale when you add countries: their price levels differ by many powers of ten.

**What to notice.**

- Prices rose slowly until the mid-1960s, much faster in the 1970s and early 1980s, and then at a
  steadier pace, until the jump of 2021–2022.
- On the linear scale the line rises about as steeply in the 2000s as in the 1970s, because the same
  percentage increase adds more index points when prices are already high. Switch to the ratio scale:
  there the slope is the *percentage* rate of change, and the 1970s clearly stand out.
- Add Japan: its deflator *fell* from 119 in 1994 to 100 in 2013, two decades of deflation. Add Turkey on the
  ratio scale: its price level in 2025 was more than 30,000 times its 1990 level.

> **Python note.** With dates as row labels, `level["1965"]` picks the four quarters of 1965, and
> `.mean()` averages them. The formula $(\text{end}/\text{start})^{1/\text{years}} - 1$ is the average
> annual growth rate.

```{python}
level = deflator.set_index("date").gdp_deflator_2012_100
for start, end in [(1947, 1965), (1965, 1983), (1983, 2019), (2019, 2025)]:
    yearly = (level[str(end)].mean() / level[str(start)].mean()) ** (1 / (end - start)) - 1
    print(f"{start}-{end}: prices rose {yearly:.1%} a year on average")
```

#### Key numbers: nominal GDP = price level × real GDP

The textbook asks how much more real GDP the United States produced in 2022 than in 1995. Real GDP in
our national accounts file is measured in chained 2017 dollars.

```{python}
nominal_ratio = nipa.loc[2022, "gdp"] / nipa.loc[1995, "gdp"]
real_ratio = nipa.loc[2022, "real_gdp"] / nipa.loc[1995, "real_gdp"]
print(f"Nominal GDP: ${nipa.loc[1995, 'gdp'] / 1000:.1f} trillion (1995), ${nipa.loc[2022, 'gdp'] / 1000:.1f} trillion (2022)")
print(f"Nominal GDP grew by a factor of {nominal_ratio:.2f}")
print(f"Real GDP grew by a factor of    {real_ratio:.2f}")
print(f"So the price level grew by      {nominal_ratio / real_ratio:.2f}")
```

Nominal GDP more than tripled, but real GDP did not quite double: the rest of the rise came from a
price level that went up by about three-quarters. (The textbook's \$7.4 trillion for 1995 is now \$7.6 trillion after
revisions.)

Taking growth rates of equation (4) gives a handy approximation (equation 7): the growth of nominal GDP is about
the growth of the price level plus the growth of real GDP.

> **Python note.** `.pct_change()` computes the change from the previous row as a fraction, for every
> row at once. The first row has no previous row, so it gets `NaN` ("not a number").

```{python}
growth = 100 * nipa[["gdp", "real_gdp"]].pct_change()
growth["prices"] = 100 * (nipa.gdp / nipa.real_gdp).pct_change()
growth["prices + real"] = growth.prices + growth.real_gdp
growth.loc[2019:].round(2)
```

In 2022, for example, nominal GDP grew 9.7 percent: prices rose 7.1 percent and real GDP 2.4 percent.
The sum, 9.6 percent, is very close. The rule is only approximate because the exact relation multiplies
growth factors: $1.097 = 1.071 \times 1.024$.
